breakfast.name: Dosa (Fermented Crepe)
breakfast.description: Crispy fermented rice and lentil crepe, served with sambar and chutney. South Indian classic requiring overnight fermentation
instructions: Soak rice and urad dal separately for 4 hours
Drain and combine rice, dal, and fenugreek seeds
Grind together with minimal water to create smooth, airy batter
Ferment batter overnight (8-12 hours) in warm place
Batter should rise and have a sour smell
Stir batter and add salt and black pepper
Heat dosa tawa (flat griddle) over medium-high heat
Lightly oil the griddle
Pour batter in spiral pattern from center outward
Spread into thin circle (about 8 inches diameter)
Drizzle oil around edges
Cook until bottom is golden and crispy (2-3 minutes)
Flip and cook other side briefly
Serve hot with sambar and coconut chutney
breakfast.notes: Fermentation is crucial for authentic taste and texture. Weather affects fermentation time—may take 8-24 hours
breakfast.fun_fact: Dosa is considered South India's answer to bread and is often eaten for breakfast or as a light dinner
alternatives: Use pre-made dosa mix to skip fermentation
Make pancake-like version without spreading thin
Fill with spiced potatoes for 'masala dosa'
stepHelp: Soaking separately matters because they grind at different rates — urad dal grinds smoother and faster than rice.

Add water a little at a time while grinding — you want a thick, pourable batter, and too much water at once makes it hard to judge the final consistency. A wet grinder incorporates more air than a blender, giving a lighter dosa.
A warm spot (like an oven with just the light on, or near a sunny window) speeds fermentation. Cold weather can double the time needed.
This is how you know it worked — the batter should look visibly bubbly and roughly doubled, with a mild tangy smell like yogurt.
Start in the center and spiral outward in one continuous motion without lifting the ladle — stopping and restarting creates thick spots.
Use the back of the ladle in light, circular strokes — the thinner you spread it, the crispier the finished dosa.
Resist the urge to press or move it — a well-fermented batter releases from the tawa naturally once it's ready to flip.

variations.title: Masala Dosa
variations.text: Fill the cooked dosa with spiced mashed potato before folding for the most popular restaurant version.

variations.title: Rava Dosa
variations.text: Swap in a semolina-based instant batter (no fermentation needed) for a lacy, crispy dosa in a fraction of the time.

variations.title: Cheese Dosa
variations.text: Sprinkle shredded cheese over the dosa right before folding for a melty, kid-friendly twist.

variations.title: Set Dosa
variations.text: Make the batter thicker and don't spread it as thin for a soft, spongy dosa instead of a crispy one.

variations.title: Onion Dosa
variations.text: Scatter finely chopped onion, green chili, and cilantro over the batter right after pouring.

serveWith.intro: A South Indian breakfast is built around dosa's crisp, tangy simplicity paired with a few punchy sides.

items.title: Sambar
items.text: A tangy, spiced lentil-vegetable stew — the traditional dipping companion for dosa.

items.title: Coconut Chutney
items.text: Cool and creamy, it balances the crisp, slightly tangy dosa.

items.title: Tomato Chutney
items.text: A tangier, spicier alternative or addition to coconut chutney.

items.title: Filter Coffee
items.text: Strong South Indian filter coffee is the classic breakfast pairing.

items.title: Podi (Spiced Lentil Powder)
items.text: Mixed with a little oil or ghee and spread on the dosa for extra flavor without needing a dip.

expertTips.title: Fermentation Time Varies With Weather
expertTips.text: In warm climates, 8 hours is plenty; in a cold kitchen it can take up to 24 — go by how the batter looks and smells, not the clock.

expertTips.title: Season the Tawa First
expertTips.text: For a new or non-seasoned tawa, rub it with a cut onion dipped in oil between dosas to keep the batter from sticking.

expertTips.title: Consistency Is Everything
expertTips.text: The batter should coat the back of a spoon like a slightly thick pancake batter — too thin and it won't spread into a solid circle, too thick and it won't crisp.

expertTips.title: Medium-High, Not High Heat
expertTips.text: Too hot and the dosa browns before it cooks through; too low and it never crisps. Medium-high is the sweet spot.

storage.title: Fridge
storage.text: Fermented batter keeps in the fridge for up to 4-5 days — fermentation slows but doesn't stop, so the batter gets tangier over time.

storage.title: Freezer
storage.text: Freeze extra batter in an airtight container for up to 1 month; thaw in the fridge overnight before using.

storage.title: Cooked Dosa
storage.text: Cooked dosas don't keep well — they're best made fresh to order, right as you plan to eat them.

breakfast.makeAhead: The batter is the make-ahead part: mix and start fermenting it the night before you want dosa (or up to 2 days ahead, refrigerated after the initial ferment). Having a bowl of ready batter in the fridge means fresh dosa is just a few minutes away any morning.

faqs.q: My batter didn't rise — what went wrong?
faqs.a: Likely the kitchen was too cold; this fermentation relies on ambient warmth. Try a warmer spot, or extend the fermentation time — it can take up to 24 hours in cold weather.
You'll lose the characteristic tang and airy texture, but a same-day batter still cooks into a serviceable, denser dosa — rava dosa is a better instant option if you're short on time.

faqs.q: Why does my dosa stick to the pan?
faqs.a: The tawa likely isn't hot enough or well-seasoned. Make sure it's fully preheated and lightly but evenly oiled before each dosa.

faqs.q: Can I use a blender instead of a wet grinder?
faqs.a: Yes, though a wet grinder traditionally produces a lighter, airier batter — a blender works fine, just grind in batches so it doesn't overheat the batter.

lunch.name: Biryani (Layered Rice and Meat)
lunch.description: Fragrant basmati rice layered with spiced meat or vegetables and cooked in sealed pot. India's most festive dish
ingredients: 1.5 lbs chicken, mutton, or beef, cubed
instructions: Soak saffron in hot milk
Fry sliced onions in ghee until golden and crispy, set aside 1/2 for garnish
In remaining ghee, add whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, bay, cloves) and toast
Add cubed meat and cook on high heat for 2 minutes
Mix yogurt with garlic, ginger, green chili, salt, and pepper
Add yogurt mixture to meat and cook 15 minutes, stirring
Parboil rice in salted water until 70% cooked (about 5 minutes)
In heavy-bottomed pot, layer meat mixture at bottom
Top with half the parboiled rice
Layer remaining meat
Top with remaining rice
Sprinkle saffron milk, fried onions, and cilantro on top
Cover pot tightly with foil, then lid (trap steam inside)
Cook on high heat for 1-2 minutes until steam forms
Reduce heat to low and cook 30-40 minutes
Turn off heat and let sit 10 minutes without opening
Open carefully and fluff with fork
lunch.notes: The dum pukht (steaming) method is essential. Never open the pot during cooking or steam escapes
lunch.fun_fact: Biryani arrived in India with Muslim rulers and became a symbol of celebration and royalty. Each region has its own style
alternatives: Vegetable biryani with potatoes and peas
Pressure cooker method for faster cooking
Different meat: goat, fish, or shrimp
Brown rice instead of white for healthier option

dinner.name: Chicken Tikka Masala
dinner.description: Chunks of chicken marinated and cooked in tandoor-style oven, then simmered in creamy tomato sauce
instructions: Mix yogurt with ginger-garlic paste, cumin, coriander, turmeric, chili powder, and salt
Marinate chicken in this mixture for 30 minutes (or longer)
Heat ghee in pan over high heat and cook chicken tikka until slightly charred
Remove chicken and set aside
In same pan, add chopped onion and cook until golden
Add tomato sauce and simmer for 5 minutes
Add heavy cream and stir well
Add garam masala powder
Return cooked chicken to sauce
Simmer 15-20 minutes until sauce thickens
Garnish with fresh cilantro
Serve with naan bread or rice
dinner.notes: For tandoor effect, broil marinated chicken in oven at 500°F for 8-10 minutes before adding to sauce
dinner.fun_fact: Chicken Tikka Masala is often called the national dish of Britain, invented by British-Indian restaurants in the 1960s-70s
alternatives: Paneer (cottage cheese) for vegetarian version
Greek yogurt instead of heavy cream
Coconut milk instead of cream
Use whole chicken pieces instead of cubes

snacks.name: Samosa (Fried Pastry Triangle)
snacks.description: Crispy fried pastry pocket filled with spiced potatoes and peas. Popular Indian street food and appetizer
instructions: Make dough: Mix flour, salt, turmeric, and ghee
Add warm water gradually until stiff dough forms
Knead 5 minutes and cover for 30 minutes
Make filling: Heat 1 tbsp oil, add cumin seeds
Add chopped onion and cook until soft
Add mashed potatoes, peas, coriander, garam masala, chili, amchur
Mix well and season with salt. Cool filling
Divide dough into 12 balls
Roll each ball thin and cut in half to create semicircles
Roll each semicircle into cone shape, sealing edges with water
Fill with 1-2 tbsp spiced potato mixture
Fold top corner down and seal with water
Heat oil to 350°F
Deep fry samosas in batches until golden brown
Drain on paper towels
Serve hot with tamarind chutney or mint chutney
snacks.notes: The dough must be stiff to form crispy shells. Samosas can be baked instead of fried
snacks.fun_fact: Samosas are believed to have originated in the Middle East and came to India through trade routes
alternatives: Meat-filled samosas with ground lamb
Baked instead of fried for healthier option
Phyllo dough instead of homemade pastry
Vegetable samosas with cabbage and carrots

desserts.name: Gulab Jamun (Rose Syrup Balls)
desserts.description: Soft milk dough balls soaked in fragrant rose and cardamom syrup
instructions: Mix powdered milk, flour, and baking soda
Knead with 2-3 tbsp milk to make soft dough
Divide into 12 balls, roll smooth in palm
Heat ghee to 350°F
Deep fry balls until light brown, about 2 minutes
Remove with slotted spoon
In separate pot, combine sugar and water
Bring to boil and simmer 5 minutes to create syrup
Add cardamom powder and rose water
Stir in saffron strands
Drop fried balls into warm syrup immediately
Let soak for 1 hour minimum before serving
Garnish with sliced pistachios
Serve at room temperature or chilled
desserts.notes: Balls must be soaked in warm syrup while still hot. Store in syrup in refrigerator
desserts.fun_fact: Gulab Jamun is often called the king of Indian desserts and is essential at celebrations and weddings
alternatives: Condensed milk instead of powdered milk
Dry milk powder from grocery store
Orange blossom water instead of rose water
Different nuts for garnish: almonds or cashews

drinks.name: Indian Chai (Spiced Tea)
drinks.description: Strong black tea with aromatic spices and milk, a beloved Indian beverage
instructions: Bring water to boil in saucepan
Add cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and ginger
Simmer for 2 minutes
Add black tea leaves
Simmer for 1-2 minutes
Add milk and sugar
Bring back to boil
Strain into cups
Add pinch of salt if desired
Serve immediately
drinks.notes: The spices should be added to water first for maximum flavor extraction
drinks.fun_fact: Chai is central to Indian social life and hospitality. Tea vendors on streets are iconic across India
alternatives: Different spice combinations based on preference
Condensed milk instead of regular milk
Honey instead of sugar
Green cardamom instead of black cardamom

drinks.name: Lassi (Yogurt Drink) - Non-Alcoholic Version
drinks.description: Refreshing yogurt-based drink served chilled, either sweet or savory
instructions: Pour yogurt into blender
Add milk and sugar
Add cardamom powder
Blend until smooth
Add ice cubes and blend again
Strain if desired for smoother texture
Serve immediately in chilled glasses
Optional: Add rose water and saffron for special occasions
drinks.notes: For savory lassi, use salt instead of sugar and add roasted cumin powder
drinks.fun_fact: Lassi is served after meals in Indian cuisine to aid digestion and cool the palate
alternatives: Mango lassi with fresh mango puree
Strawberry lassi for fruity version
Savory lassi with salt and cumin
Coconut milk instead of regular milk
